A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Craftium framework by the same authors. All text, figures and tables are readable, including v2's Appendices A–I. V1 has no appendices. The substantial expansion supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 presents framework and task descriptions, code examples and illustrative screenshots, but reports no original experimental measurements or evaluation outcomes.

after.justification: V2 reports original throughput and memory measurements, learning curves, multi-agent self-play, open-world agent comparisons, prompt experiments and continual-learning results in Sections 3.4–3.5 and Appendices E and G.

M1.justification: V1 leaves multi-agent interaction and PettingZoo integration as future work. V2 implements them through per-agent communication channels and clients coordinated by the engine server (Section 3, Figure 2 and Appendix D). It also introduces a parameterized dungeon-generation algorithm (Appendix G.4). These are substantive procedural additions, independent of the engine terminology change.

E1.justification: The five original single-agent task types are retained. V2 additionally evaluates one-versus-one combat, an open world with resource-gathering, hunting and defense objectives, and a ten-task continual-learning dungeon sequence (Section 3.5 and Appendix G). These substantially expand the evaluated task requirements and interaction settings.

E2.justification: V1 discusses alternatives without evaluating comparators. V2 benchmarks Craftium against MineDojo and VizDoom for single-environment throughput and against VizDoom for parallel throughput. Its demonstrations also compare PPO+LSTM with LLaVa-Agent and from-scratch PPO (FS) with continual fine-tuning using L2 regularization (FT-L2).

E3.justification: Reported episode limits change substantially: ChopTree and Room increase from 500 to 2,000 steps, SmallRoom from 200 to 1,000, Speleo from 500 to 3,000, and SpidersAttack from 2,000 to 4,000 (v1 Section 3.4; v2 Appendix G.1). V2 also introduces throughput-testing and learning protocols, including million-step PPO training and open-world comparisons with different observation formats and time/step budgets.

E4.justification: V1 contains no corresponding analyses. V2 tests throughput sensitivity to parallel environment count, frame skipping, observation resolution, world complexity and agent count (Appendix E, Figure 13). It also compares four LLaVa-Agent prompts to select the demonstration prompt (Appendix G.3, Figure 17).

E5.justification: V2 introduces repeated-run and uncertainty reporting absent from v1: five-run throughput measurements with means and standard deviations in Table 4, five-run learning curves with standard errors in Figures 8 and 15, ten random seeds for the open-world comparison, and five repetitions per prompt. These are newly reported experiments, not increased repetitions of v1 results.

E6.justification: V1 reports no measured performance. V2 adds throughput means of 2,746.69, 2,091.91 and 71.87 steps/s for Craftium, VizDoom and MineDojo respectively (Table 4), plus over 12,000 steps/s in a parallel configuration (Figure 13a). It also adds learning curves, open-world achievements and task-dependent FS/FT-L2 results. These are new findings, not same-setting improvements over v1 measurements.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results, formal assumptions or proofs. V2's additional action-space notation explains existing controls, while its new generator descriptions concern implementation rather than substantive mathematical analysis.

C1.justification: V2 expands the main contribution from a customizable RL environment framework to an efficient platform for single-agent, multi-agent, embodied and continual-learning research. It adds quantitative efficiency claims and claims novelty in combining vast 3D open worlds with multi-agent support. The original five environments, presented partly as benchmarks in v1, are explicitly reframed as illustrative examples.

C2.justification: V2 adds proposed explanations for throughput differences, interprets selected continual-learning gains as forward transfer, and discusses richness–efficiency tradeoffs. It newly states that agent count is limited by CPU-core count and qualifies the learning demonstrations as untuned examples whose performance may improve with longer training (Appendices E and G).

D1.justification: Beyond v1's basic mod and Gymnasium examples, v2 documents engine modifications, action mappings, API functions and PettingZoo usage (Appendices A–D). It adds benchmark hardware, CleanRL implementation and commit references, preprocessing, budgets, prompts, generator parameters and an environment-creation tutorial (Appendices E, G and I). The project repository link is retained.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning toward embodied AI, continual learning, open-endedness and multi-agent research, adding discussion of works such as Habitat 3.0, Craftax, OMNI-EPIC and JaxMARL. Table 1 introduces a structured framework comparison, while Appendices F and H expand the arguments concerning VizDoom's dimensional limitations and MineDojo's customization restrictions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, background, related work and conclusion are substantially rewritten around flexibility, efficiency and broader autonomous-agent applications. Section 3 gains dedicated performance and illustrative-example sections. The original task descriptions move to Appendix G.1 within a new, extensive appendix structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text to a two-column layout and redraws Figure 2 for the multi-agent architecture. It adds performance and learning plots, maps, a skills tree, comparison/API/prompt tables and tutorial screenshots. The original five-task image panel is retained and reordered as Figure 14, rather than being removed.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves v1's central evidential gap: a largely descriptive framework proposal gains measured performance comparisons, learning demonstrations and sensitivity analyses (Sections 3.4–3.5; Appendices E and G). Its implementation and usage documentation also becomes substantially more complete. Different benchmark tasks/resolutions and unequal open-world budgets limit broad superiority conclusions, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and practical assessability.
